initial_observation.encounter_context: presentation for evaluation of recurrent aseptic meningitis with multiple episodes over 18 years
initial_observation.chief_complaint: recurrent aseptic meningitis first presenting 18 years ago
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The patient had 121 episodes of recurrent aseptic meningitis starting 18 years prior, with prior history of recurrent urticaria and arthralgia since age 30; episodes started occurring several times a year from age 53 with preceding low-grade fever, general fatigue, arthralgia and urticaria then high fever and headache; white blood cell count and C reactive protein levels were normal or mildly elevated during meningitis; cerebrospinal fluid showed >1000 polymorphonuclear leucocytes/mm3; no bacteria, fungi, or mycobacteria cultured; PCR negative for herpesviruses and enteroviruses; urticarial biopsy showed neutrophil infiltration; corticosteroids shortened attack duration but did not prevent recurrence; colchicine trial without evidence of familial Mediterranean fever; genetic analysis showed no mutations in MEFV, MVK, TNFRSF1A, NLRP3 or NLRP12

evidence_items.source_text: Examination of the lumbar cerebrospinal fluid demonstrated >1000 polymorphonuclear leucocytes/mm3. No bacteria, fungi or mycobacteria were cultured. PCR tests were negative for herpesviruses and enteroviruses.
White blood cell count and C reactive protein levels were normal or mildly elevated during the meningitis period (table 1). The test results for various autoantibodies were negative.
A biopsy from urticarial lesion showed neutrophil infiltration.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: during clinical course before PNH diagnosis

evidence_items.source_text: Genetic analysis revealed no mutations in MEFV, MVK, TNFRSF1A, NLRP3 and NLRP12.

Meningitis started occurring more frequently and was accompanied by sudden brownish urine and occasionally by altered consciousness, which lasted for several days. At the age of 68, the patient developed severe haemolysis. Haemoglobin declined to 8.2 g/dL and lactate dehydrogenase elevated up to 3004 IU/L. He also developed acute renal failure because of the deposition of haemosiderin in renal tubules. Serum creatinine increased from 2.8 to 8.65 mg/dL. He required temporary haemodialysis for a month until his condition improved.

A bone marrow study revealed no sign of aplasia or hypoplasia. Flow cytometric analysis of both erythrocytes and granulocytes revealed deficiency of CD59 and CD55, glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein, and he was diagnosed with PNH in addition to recurrent meningitis (figure 2A).

Genetic analysis was performed after obtaining approval from the ethical committee and the patient’s informed consent. The analysis of the genes involved in GPI anchor synthesis showed no mutations in PIGA, but revealed a nonsense germ-line mutation (c.250G>T, p.E84X), and single-nucleotide polymorphism array analysis revealed a somatic 18 Mbp deletion in chromosome 20q including PIGT (figure 2B, C).
The patient was administered eculizumab, an anti-C5 antibody, immediately after the diagnosis.
All the symptoms, such as urticaria, arthralgia, headache and haemolysis, completely disappeared due to regulated administration of eculizumab. The remission has lasted for 3 years as of now.
